newsitem.title: USA: GM to renovate Detroit headquarters for city use.
newsitem.headline: GM to renovate Detroit headquarters for city use.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and the city of Detroit have agreed to pursue a renovation of GM's historic headquarters building for use as the new municipal government centre, city and company officials said Tuesday.

Mayor Dennis Archer and GM Chairman Jack Smith said the complex transaction also would include renovation of the current office space occupied by the city government for use as first-class office space in downtown Detroit.
In addition, GM and the United Auto Workers union plan to construct a new, 300,000-square foot training centre for GM hourly employees in downtown Detroit.
In May, GM announced that it would purchase the Renaissance Centre for use as its worldwide corporate headquarters, a move that left the future of its 76-year-old headquarters building in doubt.

That move also is expected to displace hundreds of commercial tenants now occupying the Renaissance Centre as the automaker moves its offices into the complex. One of the biggest tenants in the RenCen, as the complex is known locally, is Ford Motor Co.

The plans announced Tuesday, if consummated, would provide a future use for the GM Building, as well as about 350,000 square feet of new office space to accommodate current Renaissance Centre tenants.
"This city is our home and we want to make it better," GM's Smith said. "We are playing our part in pulling the city together, not only symbolically, but geographically and economically."
Funding for the multi-million dollar renovations has not yet been decided, but Archer said the city does not intend to pay any of the costs.
Matthew Cullen, GM's director of worldwide real estate said the automaker intends to convey its old headquarters to a developer free of cost, who will then arrange financing for the project.
Cullen said he does not anticipate that the project would be paid for with a bond issue, but rather through private financing and anticipated rent revenues from the city and other tenants.
"It's a market driven real estate transaction," Cullen said.
